outline.description: Sets the stage by detailing the petitioners’ personal history, the threats they faced in Colombia, and the procedural journey through the immigration court, BIA, and the appellate court.
subtopics: 1.1. Petitioners’ biographical facts and political activities in Colombia
1.2. The property dispute and encounters with “Don Rafa” and his criminal network
1.3. Sequence of threats, assaults, and the family’s flight to the United States
1.4. Initial removal proceedings: Notices to Appear, IJ denial, and BIA affirmation
1.5. Scope of the appellate review: issues preserved and issues waived

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 2: Governing Law and Standard of Review
outline.description: Explains the statutory framework for asylum and withholding of removal, the burden of proof, and the appellate court’s review standards under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and relevant precedent.
subtopics: 2.1. Definition of refugee and elements of asylum under the INA
2.2. Elements required for withholding of removal
2.3. Burden of proof: preponderance of the evidence for asylum, clear and convincing for withholding
2.4. Standard of review for BIA findings: substantial‑evidence standard for facts, de novo for legal conclusions
2.5. Key precedent governing review (Singh v. Bondi; Rivera‑Barrientos; Uanreroro v. Gonzales)

outline.description: Analyzes the court’s evaluation of whether the petitioners suffered past persecution, focusing on the nature of threats, cumulative harm, and the requirement that persecution be more than mere threats.
subtopics: 3.1. Legal definition of persecution in the Ninth Circuit and its application in the Tenth Circuit
3.2. The cumulative‑effects approach versus isolated‑incident analysis
3.3. Review of the petitioners’ alleged harms: phone threats, gunpoint encounters, assault on a factory employee, and psychological impact
3.4. Controlling cases on threats versus persecution (Karki v. Holder; Brandy v. Holder; Chhetri v. Rosen)
3.5. Court’s finding of insufficient substantial evidence to meet the persecution element

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 4: Nexus to a Protected Ground – Political Opinion
outline.description: Breaks down the nexus requirement, the need for a protected ground to be a central motive, and why the court concluded the petitioners’ political opinion was tangential.
subtopics: 4.1. Nexus requirement under 8 U.S.C. § 1158(b)(1)(B)(i)
4.2. “Central reason” test and its application in mixed‑motive cases
4.3. Evidence of motive: threats tied to Jimenez’s investigation of Don Rafa’s property versus political campaigning
4.4. Comparison to Tenth Circuit precedent on nexus (Dallakoti v. Holder; Yuk v. Ashcroft)
4.5. Court’s conclusion that the primary motive was personal/retributive, not political

outline.chapter_title: Chapter 5: Government Protection, Internal Relocation, and the Final Holding
outline.description: Covers the analysis of the “unable or unwilling” prong, the internal relocation inquiry, and synthesizes how these findings lead to the denial of asylum and withholding of removal.
subtopics: 5.1. Legal framework for government protection (Singh; Aviles‑Gonzalez)
5.2. The importance of reporting to authorities and evidentiary burden
5.3. Evaluation of petitioners’ interactions with Colombian police and lack of systemic evidence of inability or unwillingness
5.4. Internal relocation standard under 8 C.F.R. § 1208.13(b)(1)(i) and case law (Rivera‑Barrientos)
5.5. Summary of the court’s holdings: denial of asylum, denial of withholding of removal, and affirmation of the BIA’s decision
